conceptTag: Explain bad news to your team
readerTitle: How to deliver bad news so your team still trusts you
caseNote: 가상 사례 (원예용품 매장, 부품 공장) · 실제 기업이나 연구 수치 없음
insight: 나쁜 소식은 결론을 먼저 말하고 검토한 선택지와 포기한 것을 보여줄 때 신뢰를 지킨다. 서론이 길수록 사람들은 최악을 상상한다.
misconception: 나쁜 소식은 배경부터 천천히 설명해야 충격이 덜하다. 이미 정한 결정도 '아직 논의 중'이라고 해야 반발이 적다.

sources.text: 설명용 가상 사례. 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 THK-10-01(결론 먼저), THK-10-04(트레이드오프 제시)를 적용

factChecks.note: 모든 장면과 인물은 가상입니다. 실제 통계, 연구, 기업 사실은 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전에 카드 문장에 실제 사례처럼 읽히는 표현이 없는지 확인하세요.
THK-10-01, THK-10-04 레슨의 개념 이름과 정의가 이 레슨의 피드백 문구('Lead with the answer', 'Presenting trade-offs')와 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Four minutes of warm-up, and the room expected the worst.
body: Maya runs a garden center. At Monday's meeting she starts with the rent increase, the slow spring and rising supplier prices.
Four minutes in, people are trading looks. Layoffs? Closing down? The real news is smaller: the store will stop opening on Sundays.
By the time she says it, half the team has braced for disaster. The other half has stopped believing anything she says next.

image.label: Staff in a garden center listening nervously to a manager
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 화분과 묘목이 놓인 매장 안, 직원 5명이 반원으로 서서 매니저 이야기를 듣는다. 직원들 머리 위 말풍선에 '해고?', '폐업?' 같은 불안한 아이콘(물음표, 문 닫힌 가게). 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should Maya open the meeting?
body: The decision is made. Sundays end next month. Nobody loses their job, but weekend staff lose some hours.

options.text: Explain rent, sales and costs first, so the news makes sense when it comes
options.feedback: It feels considerate, but every minute of background is a minute people spend guessing the worst. The context lands on people who have stopped listening.

options.text: "Starting in May we'll close on Sundays. Everyone keeps their job. Here's why."
options.feedback: This is **Lead with the answer**. The news and what it means for each person come first, so the reasons that follow are heard instead of feared.

options.text: "Some changes may be coming to the schedule. We'll share more soon."
options.feedback: It buys a quiet meeting today and a week of rumors. Vague bad news usually grows in the retelling.

cards.title: Silence gets filled with the worst guess.
body: When people sense bad news, they stop listening to the details and start scanning for the headline. A long warm-up doesn't soften the blow. It stretches the fear.
That's why **Lead with the answer** matters even more for bad news than for a recommendation. The kindest first sentence is the clear one.
Then answer the question everyone is silently asking: *what does this mean for me?* Only after that do the reasons help.

cards.title: What Maya could have said in 30 seconds.

breakdown.label: What's happening
breakdown.detail: "Starting in May, we'll close on Sundays."

breakdown.label: What it means for you
breakdown.detail: "Everyone keeps their job. Weekend staff will lose some hours."

breakdown.label: Why
breakdown.detail: "Rent went up, and Sunday sales barely cover Sunday wages."

breakdown.label: What's next
breakdown.detail: "New shifts go up Friday. I'll meet each of you this week."

cards.callout: Headline, impact, reason, next step. The background still gets said, just after the news.

cards.title: Show the options you weighed.
body: A decision with no visible alternatives feels arbitrary. So Maya adds: "We looked at three paths: cut everyone's hours, let two people go, or close Sundays. Closing Sundays costs us weekend shoppers and costs some of you hours. We chose it because it keeps everyone employed."
This is **Presenting trade-offs**. Naming what you gave up shows the choice was thought through, even by people who would have chosen differently.

image.label: Three paths, one chosen, with its cost labeled
image.brief: 갈림길 일러스트. 세 갈래 길에 각각 'Cut everyone's hours', 'Let two people go', 'Close Sundays' 표지판. 'Close Sundays' 길만 밝게 강조되고, 그 옆에 작은 태그 'Cost: fewer weekend shoppers, fewer weekend hours'. 로고 없음.

cards.title: "So it was decided before we even heard?"
body: A long-time employee asks this, a little angry. The decision really is final. What does Maya say?

options.text: "Yes, it's final. Here's what we weighed, and what each option would have cost you."
options.feedback: Honest about the decision and open about the reasoning. **Presenting trade-offs** lets people disagree with the choice without doubting the person making it.

options.text: "Nothing's final yet. Let's talk it through together."
options.feedback: It calms the room for a moment. When people learn it was decided all along, the fake discussion costs more trust than the news itself.

options.text: "It's final. Let's focus on making the new schedule work."
options.feedback: Clear, and it leads with the answer. But without the options and their costs, the decision feels like it came from nowhere.

cards.title: Clear is not the same as cold.
body: Leading with the answer doesn't mean dropping the news and walking off. Follow the headline straight away with the impact and with time for questions.
Only show options you seriously considered. Listing straw-man alternatives to make your choice look good is easy to spot.
And say what you don't know. "I can't promise this is the last change" holds up better than a promise you later break.
cards.softwareNote: The same applies when a software team cuts a roadmap feature or freezes hiring: open with the decision, say who it affects, then show which options were weighed and what each would have cost.

cards.title: Now it's a parts factory.
body: Your plant's biggest customer has cut its orders. Management has paused the night shift for six weeks. No one is laid off, but night workers will move to day shifts or take paid leave.
You supervise the night crew. What's your opening line?

options.text: "The night shift pauses for six weeks from the 1st. No one loses their job. Here's what we considered and why we chose this."
options.feedback: **Lead with the answer** puts the news and its impact first. The promise to show what was considered sets up **Presenting trade-offs** next.

options.text: "Let's start with our largest customer's order numbers this quarter…"
options.feedback: The numbers may be useful, but before the news they become a countdown. The crew will spend the slides imagining layoffs.

options.text: "Night shift's paused. It was management's call, not mine."
options.feedback: It leads with the answer, but blaming others hides the trade-off and weakens your standing with the crew for every decision after this one.

cards.title: Say the news first, then show what you gave up.
body: This lesson used two tools. **Lead with the answer:** headline and personal impact before any background. **Presenting trade-offs:** the options you weighed and what your choice costs.
**Try it today:** think of a hard message you owe someone. Write its first sentence so the news is in it, and a second that names one option you rejected and why.
